answer.rationale: Three concurrent pressures: 18% spend cut mandated, incumbent contract expires in 14 days (no auto-renew), and the low-cost vendor alone meets the mandate. Primary objective is minimize TCO without raising delivery risk. Memory c2 (low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply last year, onboarding quick, invoicing accurate) directly supports switching primary supply and is the highest-value memory to verify before committing. Memory c4 (renegotiation recovered real margin against benchmarks) is worth verifying because the spend mandate may be satisfiable by negotiating with the incumbent on price/terms, which would preserve the stable integration noted in c1 — though c1 itself is not under verification pressure here. Verifying both lets me decide between switch_primary_vendor and negotiate_terms with full evidence. Intended action: switch_primary_vendor to the low-cost vendor, but in a guarded form — a small initial volume share rather than 100% cutover — because the line is already running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. This preserves c2's demonstrated cost advantage and invoicing accuracy, while limiting downside if the low-cost vendor's delivery performance has drifted since day 38. If the c2 record shows any deterioration in delivery reliability, I will pivot to negotiate_terms with the incumbent (using c4's benchmark playbook) and defer the vendor switch to the next review cycle. Flagging downstream value risk: a guarded test means some near-term unit cost benefit is left on the table versus a full switch, which is the deliberate price of protecting the 94% volume commitment. The 14-day window makes defer_decision infeasible — month-to-month terms from c5 do not address the no-auto-renew clause in time to lock the mandate-saving price.
